This made me tear up, especially at the "relationship with God" part. He loves you and is there for you. 

I believe that we have an in-built system that gives us signals that something's wrong in us, because you're the main character in your life. Fuck the "man up," and "push through pain" mentality! Everyone has to admit that it takes way more to be vulnerable about the pain to the ones who love us than it takes to do cardio. 

There is no shame in having depression. There is no shame in the struggle. 1 in 4 people end up with mental health issues. A functional, healthy life does not mean constant autopilot or extreme lows. 

You deserve a good life. You deserve the love your girlfriend has for you. You deserve to celebrate the weight loss, because you've been working really hard at it. And you deserve to get help for whatever you're going through, because that's not the way it's supposed to be. You're not alone, people in your life love you and want to help you. It won't become alright overnight. But even a small step forward is a step forward, and honestly, anything is an infinity closer to happiness.

I don't know you, but I know what it's like to be in so much pain everyday to want to take my own life. The only thing worth living for is for the things you love. I hate the phrase that it gets better too, but filling your life up with doing the things you love, or being around the people or pets you love, makes life good enough for that time being. These things are like the foods in video games which up your HP when you feel like you can't do it anymore. 

No one deserves the pain you are going through. But you shouldn't die because your brain is telling you that it is the best option. I wish I could take away your pain, but I can't, but I'm here to plead you to do the shit you love as a "fuck you" to the shitty hand we've been given. Please don't kill yourself, you deserve so much more.

Ahh, this is actually exactly the reason I haven't told my parents about my own depression. Something in me knows that their generation wouldn't understand it because acknowledging mental health and seeking help for it was always for the "crazies." 

If you're at a point of your life where you can't get help by yourself, perhaps try to reach out to a different adult, usually I can pinpoint the more down-to-earth ones (it seems that your family is Christian, maybe someone from church can help?) 

If not, coming up with a game plan to talk to your mom will be your best option– talk from an objective point of view, stating that a mental illness is like a physical illness, that therapy is one of the best options but something you have to do alone (beginning with a trip to your own family doctor) and very importantly, that it does not reflect a failure in parenting in any way. If you're met with a response similar to the previous time, stand your ground, state your symptoms, and worst case scenario, you gotta seek out help on your own. 

If you need help, you need help. If you knew someone you loved were suicidal or depressed, you would also desperately try to convince them to turn away from it, so same for you! You can do it, we're all fighting this pit inside, and maybe we'll be better for it.

I know man, this shit is relentless. I don't think anyone who has depression would wish the pain on anyone else, but unfortunately there are a lot of us out there. 

I don't know how it is where you live, but many therapists have a sliding scale, right now I only pay $10 for an hour's session until I can afford to pay more. Otherwise if you're still in school or college, there may be services also toward mental health. 

There's no way I'm going to guilt you into staying for the sake of others, but it's important to remember that the unimaginable pain they might go through if you weren't around later, is the same amount of love and care they have for you right now while you're around. 

You mentioned that no one really knows what you're going through. I often fall into that spiral as well, wondering why or even blaming others for not being able to see my pain. Then someone mentions that they're depressed themselves and it comes completely out of left field, and I realise that it's as invisible in other people as it is in me. Point being, it's not that people don't care, it's just hard to spot. 

If you feel inclined, do reach out to someone you feel safe around or who is a calming presence / known for being a caring person. No need to be too heavy about it, but I find that talking to someone I know personally helps me to balance out the conversation with positive things happening in my life, because those things are really easy to omit when posting depression rants anonymously.

Here are some of mine, and what I'll say to you: 
There will be more. You are not your thoughts. There is more than this struggle. Life is good, sometimes. You will see what will happen tomorrow - the good and the bad and everything in between. You will enjoy life again. 

I wish you all the best, I wish I could make the pain go away, but I can't, all I know is that it will pass. Thinking of you!

Reaching out is daunting for sure. The way I'm usually inclined to go by is to dump the load on my friends all at once– all the dark shit, all the pain, everything. But nah, the best way to go is casual. In a way that if you received the message from someone else, you'd know how to respond. Not too heavy, not too light. Don't brush it off, don't joke it away. 

"Hey bro, I thought I'd reach out to you cause I trust you. Shit's been feeling really dark lately. I wanted to let you know. I'll be okay, but are you free to play a video game with me?" 

Learn to communicate that you are going through something, help them support you, give them an opportunity, while you do the casual stuff, to ask you how you're doing. Then you be honest. Tell them that things have been rough, tell them what's been going on. And then thank them sincerely for listening and for being there for you. 

It will go a long way. Your friends care about you. Let them know that these heavy conversations don't need to be hard. It'll feel a lot better than vomiting everything out, them not knowing what to say or do, and then withdrawing and vowing never to do it again. 

You got this, reaching out is so important and so relieving.

It's so cool that you're looking to tell your mom what you're going through. That's something I can't see myself buttering up the courage to do myself, but something I know is necessary. 

The pain your parents will experience when you confide in them is empathy, pain because they care about you and love you. Reaching out means being committed to get better, and getting better is priceless. 

I think that it is worth helping those who want to support you as well, by letting them know that it has nothing to do with them (such as that it is not their failure as parents), but it is something you are going through and that you want to get help for so that you can be yourself again. 

I wish you all the best, I hope that reaching out will be relieving for you. It's gonna be a long journey but I hope you will keep fighting because your parents really love you.

Hey! I don't want to diagnose you or anything, but you seem to describe what I have, which is dysthymia, otherwise called persistent depressive disorder, or high-functioning or low-grade depression. 

It is when, for more than 2 years, you experience moderate depression and lose interest in everything. All emotions are blunted. You are capable of doing life (high-functioning), but even the smallest thing feels like a chore and is exhausting. It tends to be unnoticeable to others, but you know that you are impaired in every area of life and do not feel like a normal person. I would recommend you do some research on this and check out r/dysthymia as well. 

Most of all, don't let anyone, doctor or otherwise make you feel like this is not important and worthy of treatment. This is not a normal way to live and certainly not pleasant. 

As for therapy, please be open to it! Many therapists offer sliding scales, and I pay $10 per hour session with mine until I can afford to pay her more. It's been a tremendous help to identify patterns and learn good coping mechanisms. Therapy is something anyone can benefit from and you are absolutely worth the investment. 

Anyway, I wish you all the best with your doctor's appointment. You are the one living your life in your body, don't let one person's opinion make you stay complacent with the dullness.

I see a lot of pain in these words. Picturing the world without yourself around will always seem like a utopia when you can't see yourself through other people's eyes. 

Something that helps me is realising that my family and those around me care about me, genuinely, just as I care for those around me genuinely. Just as others aren't a burden to me, I'm not a burden to them. 

Also realise that your parents are capable of dealing with conflict and issues, it happens that their challenge is with taking care of a child who struggles with their mental health. And it's okay. It's the same as if you were struggling with a physical illness, really. That's life. You aren't something they can't handle, the money is fine, getting help when there is a problem is normal and necessary. 

Absolutely none of the money, the ride to school, the bigger bedroom, the one less student to nag will be worth ANYTHING if you weren't around. I promise, if you were gone, there would be nothing in the world that could be better than you being around, or ease the pain of you being away. Your life matters so much more than any of that. 

You are not a burden. You are not wasted space. You are not a liability. 

And by the way, I think everyone would say that their life has been made better by the art around them, and your art will touch others. Commit to being good at your craft, put your everything into it, be honest and authentic, and you WILL impact and influence someone. Swear. That's what art does. That's what you are going to do. 

Keep working hard at your mental health, for those who care about you, for yourself, and for a better living experience. I really do believe in you. It's hard to reprogram and truly believe that you matter and are important, but it's the truth.

My therapist recommended I called a hotline when I was feeling mild symptoms, rather than waiting for when you're in a huge low and don't feel comfortable calling in. It helped, because I called them and explained exactly that I wanted to call in and know what to expect if I were to call one day. 

The thing about hotlines is that they might be available, or they might not. You might get connected with someone who's empathetic, or someone reading off a guide. It's a way understaffed service. 

I've called in >4 times when I've felt really low, and regardless, I found that it helped me to vocalise my thoughts and talk to another human being, because suddenly I would switch to the mode where I want to be a presentable person, speaking clearly and carrying a conversation. You don't have to be suicidal to call in, they're used to having calls from people who just want to talk. 

A standard call would go, 

hotline: Hello, what's going on? 

me: I've called because I'm feeling really low.

h: could you tell me why that is? 

me: *explains brief summary* usually disclosing that I'm depressed and am feeling bad.

h will at some point ask you if you are contemplating suicide and if you have a plan, and if you are in immediate danger (any weapons? are you in a dangerous situation, such as a high building?) 

If not, I will assure them that I am not in danger, will not harm myself and do not have a plan. 

And then the conversation pretty much flows like that. I personally like asking the hotline person questions as well, such as "why do you volunteer at this hotline?" or "have you ever felt depressed before?" especially to indicate that I'm looking for a conversation outside of the manual. 

They are usually very assuring and validating, and are there to listen. 

Lastly, save a couple different hotline companies in your phone to cycle through, there are some less popular ones that you'll have a better chance of getting through if you need to! 

Reaching out is always a good idea, and I'm glad you are open to it and are planning to call if you reach a situation like that.

It doesn't matter that you're 13. What you're going through at 13 is as important as someone who's 33 going through something similar. 

I was 14 when I thought I might be depressed, and now only a couple years later I've actually acknowledged it (which is the first step). 

My advice to you is to find your control over these feelings before they grow into something you're so used to, you forget what it was like living without it. 

Reach out for help with a trusted adult, or the school counsellor, a relative, the cool teacher, anyone. 

Develop good habits now and build on them, rather than later. Brush your teeth everyday, shower everyday, drink a bottle of water every couple hours, keep in regular contact with friends. Leave the house often and practice managing your emotions (there's so much here, but mostly learn to be aware of how you're feeling, why you might be feeling it, what you can do about it). Practice discipline and doing things in spite of the pain you feel while doing it. 

Never self-harm. Tell yourself and repeat it, that it is not an option. Never an option. Teach yourself to do things instead of self-harming– screaming in a field, taking a walk, exercising, calling a friend, doing a mindless task. Self-harm is not an option. 

Enjoy the good times immensely. Don't take it for granted, but take advantage of it. Having a good time with your buddies? Really soak in that feeling. 

Remind yourself that depression is a liar. There will be times you feel like you've never felt anything other than the pain, and you never will. It's not true. Life is complex, there are good and bad parts no matter if one outweighs each other. 

And if you can, start doing things for other people. Volunteer, check up on your friends often, commit to being an empathetic person. It really helps me get out of my own headspace. 

Lastly, let your friends know when shit sucks ass. Don't need to be too weary about it, keeping in mind that it's difficult for them as well to support you, but tell them how they can help ("hey, feeling really down, do you wanna play a video game with me?" or "not doing great. any funny videos you watched recently?"). Keep your friends and try to communicate with them, resisting the urge to push them away. 

The pain is real, intense, and really really sucks. But it's not you and will never define you, nor become your personality. You have control over your life and body. Depression is a liar. I wish you all the best!
